name: Instagram tan filter / photo editing
lead: The Instagram tan filter is a photo-editing technique in which exposure, white balance, saturation or a dedicated filter or app is used to give skin a warmer, deeper, sun-kissed colour in pictures. People use it to look healthier and more defined on camera: a darker tone tends to even out blotchiness, add contrast to the face and body, and make features such as the jaw and cheekbones read as more sculpted. Because the change happens on the image, it gives the look of a tan without UV exposure or self-tanner.

The technique belongs to the wider family of social media filters and editing apps. Wikipedia lists beauty filters that smooth skin, erase blemishes, slim the face and add virtual makeup, and editing apps such as VSCO, Snapseed, Lightroom and Facetune that adjust exposure, white balance and saturation [1]. Filters began with Japanese Purikura photo booths in 1995, Instagram added live filters in 2011, and Snapchat's 2015 purchase of Looksery brought face-tracking lenses [1].

Tanned skin has long carried associations with leisure and health in many Western countries. Wikipedia notes that this reversed a pre-1920s pattern in which a tan signalled outdoor labour, and that sunless options such as self-tanners and bronzers exist alongside UV tanning [2][8]. Researchers who study photo editing in general have examined its links with body image, and reviews report mixed findings [3][4].

angle.text: In photos, a tan filter shifts skin colour toward warmer, deeper tones, which many people use to look more even-toned and defined. The effect exists in the image only and does not change actual skin colour.

infobox: Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, editing apps such as VSCO, Snapseed, Lightroom, Facetune

paras: Editing apps adjust exposure, white balance and saturation, the settings that determine how warm and dark skin appears [1]. Some beauty filters also smooth skin, remove blemishes and under-eye bags, slim the face and add virtual makeup [1]. Users combine these controls to produce a bronzed look in a photo.

Instagram's own tools followed this pattern. A September 2011 update added new and live filters, and in February 2012 the app added Lux, an effect described as lightening shadows, darkening highlights and increasing contrast [9]. In December 2014 it added five filters named Slumber, Crema, Ludwig, Aden and Perpetua [9]. Warmer and higher-contrast looks from these tools are among the means by which people give skin a deeper tone, alongside separate editing apps [1].

The #NoFilter hashtag became popular around 2013 as a counter-trend, and users sometimes post unfiltered photos under it [1]. A study of Instagram photos by Yahoo Labs and Georgia Tech found filtered photos were 21% more likely to be viewed and 45% more likely to receive comments [1].

Wikipedia describes how tanning came into fashion in the 1920s, associated with leisure and luxury, after previously being linked with outdoor manual work; milestones include Jean Patou's first sun tan oil in 1927 and the first tanning beds in 1978 [2]. It lists self-tanning products, bronzers and spray tans as sunless routes to a tan, and notes that UV tanning is linked to sunburn, skin cancer and accelerated skin aging [2]. A photo edit gives the visual effect without any of these.

Sunless tanning products come in several forms. DHA (dihydroxyacetone) creams, lotions and sprays react with amino acids in the dead outer skin layer, and the colour fades over roughly 3 to 10 days; bronzers tint the skin until washed off [8]. The first commercial DHA self-tanner, Man-Tan, appeared in 1959, followed by Coppertone's QT in 1960, and early products were known for orange tones; reformulated products and spray booths broadened the market from the late 1990s [8]. In photos, the same warm, even look can be produced digitally.

sections.h: Research on photo editing and filters
paras: A 2022 systematic review of 22 studies on photo-editing and body concerns among women reported mixed findings and suggested a more complex relationship influenced by other factors [3]. A 2015 study in adolescent girls reported an association between self photo editing and body dissatisfaction [4]. A 2024 scoping review looked at photo manipulation and anorexia nervosa in children and adolescents and found limited evidence for that age group [5]. A randomised experiment tested whether captions disclosing that Instagram photos had been edited changed young women's mood and body image [6].

Wikipedia reports a correlation between filter use and negative body image, with the direction of causation unclear, and describes the terms 'filter dysmorphia' and 'Snapchat dysmorphia' [1]. It also reports that beauty filters tend to favour Eurocentric features such as lighter eyes and smaller noses [1]. A 2019 study linked use of Snapchat, Instagram and VSCO filters with greater acceptance of cosmetic surgery [1].

The term 'Snapchat dysmorphia' (also 'selfie dysmorphia') describes patients who seek cosmetic surgery to resemble their filtered photos. British cosmetic surgeon Tijion Esho is credited with coining it after noticing patients bringing filtered pictures of themselves rather than photos of celebrities [7]. Boston Medical Center researchers published an essay in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery in 2018 on the trend and urged surgeons to screen for body dysmorphic disorder [7]. A 2022 survey by the American Academy of Facial Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery reported that 79% of plastic surgeons saw patients wanting to look better in selfies [7].

Platform policies have shifted over time. Facebook banned filters promoting cosmetic surgery and distortion filters in 2019, and re-allowed distortion filters in 2020 [1]. In August 2020 Instagram banned filters that directly promote cosmetic surgery [7]. In August 2024 Meta announced it would remove third-party filters from its apps by January 14, 2025 [1].
No studies found on tan filters specifically. Related research on photo editing and body image is summarised above [3][4][5][6].

lore.intro: Tan filters and tan-toned edits are discussed in appearance communities as a quick way to look healthier and more defined in photos, alongside self-tanner and lighting. Claims below describe how this is framed and what research on photo editing reports.

claims.claim: A warmer, darker tone in a photo makes the face look healthier and more defined.
claims.believers: Users editing photos describe deeper tones as evening out blotchiness and adding contrast to features such as the jaw and cheekbones [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that tanned skin has been associated with leisure and health in the West since the 1920s [2]. No study has tested tan filters specifically.

claims.claim: A tan filter is a safer way to get a tanned look than UV exposure.
claims.believers: Editing gives the visual effect with no sun exposure or product on the skin.
claims.experts: UV tanning is linked to sunburn, skin cancer and accelerated skin aging [2]; sunless products such as DHA tanners are another route, with their own allergy and application cautions [8].

claims.claim: Editing your photos does not affect how you feel about your appearance.
claims.believers: Many users treat edits as a creative or aesthetic choice.
claims.experts: A 2022 systematic review reported mixed findings on photo editing and body concerns [3], and a 2015 study associated self photo editing with body dissatisfaction in adolescent girls [4].

claims.claim: Filters make people want surgery to look like their filtered selves.
claims.believers: Surgeons describe patients bringing filtered selfies as their reference, a pattern labelled 'Snapchat dysmorphia' [7].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports a correlation between filter use and negative body image, with direction of causation unclear [1]; a 2019 study linked filter use with greater acceptance of cosmetic surgery [1].

claims.claim: Telling viewers a photo was edited removes its effect on how they feel.
claims.believers: Some advocates favour disclosure captions on edited images.
claims.experts: A randomised experiment tested self-disclaimer Instagram captions on young women's mood and body image [6].

card.summary: Editing or filters to look tanner in photos; part of the wider beauty-filter trend.
card.note: Filter use in general is linked to body-image concerns.

quick.overview:
Some people use filters, editing apps or lighting to make their skin look darker or warmer in photos.

Nothing specific to tan filters has been studied.
quick.mechanism: Software adjusts colour and tone in an image; no change to actual skin occurs.
quick.risks: Research on beauty filters generally reports a correlation with negative body image, with unclear causation.[1]
